data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject rather than describes it only when the test's installation procedure itself alters the subject's execution environment in a way that the test's assertions are conditioned on, making the test a performative act that changes what it measures. The 3-of-26 result occurred because compile.py was installed under a shown-to-fail-first ritual, where the first mutation encountered was a planted failure that primed the compiler's registry state, causing 1 of 9 mutations to be silently absorbed by an ordinarily-guarded module that had already been marked as failing.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The effect disappears if the failure registry is reset between mutations","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The effect reverses if shown-to-fail-first is replaced with random mutation order","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The effect is absent in modules whose guards do not consult the shared registry","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The 1/9 loss would be 0/9 if the first mutation were not a planted failure","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The shown-to-fail-first installation creates a causal feedback loop: the test's own failure state becomes part of the subject's configuration. When compile.py encounters its first planted failure, it writes a failure marker into a shared registry that subsequent modules read as authoritative. This marker causes guard conditions in those modules to short-circuit, treating already-failing states as exempt from further validation, thereby absorbing mutations that would otherwise be caught. The asymmetry (1/9 lost vs 4/4 to 6/7 caught) reflects whether a module's guards consult the registry before or after their own checks.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
